newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Europeans taking 'easy way out' on China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Europeans taking 'easy way out' on China.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday accused unspecified European countries of "taking the easy way out" by not backing a U.N. resolution faulting China's human rights record.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns asserted an American moral high ground on the issue, and said of European Union members who oppose the resolution before the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva, "that's their problem, not ours."

"We are a country that is interested in human rights. We were built on that -- (former President Thomas) Jefferson built this country on that principle, on democracy and human rights -- and we're not going to forget it two centuries after our own birth," he said.
"The day the United States fails to stand up for human rights in the largest country in the world is the day that we will have changed as a country, and I don't believe we'll ever do that," he said.

"So other countries may decide to take the easy way out. We're not. We're going to stand up in Geneva, which is the proper forum for human rights discussion around the world, and we're going to debate this issue," he added.

An attempt last week by Denmark to push for a European Union-sponsored resolution collapsed when France said recent improvements by China on human rights suggested dialogue was better than confrontation.

The EU divisions -- coupled with Washington's delay in deciding to co-sponsor the resolution until after last week's visit to China by U.S. Vice President Al Gore -- makes it unlikely the resolution will be adopted.

Burns denied the Clinton administration was backing the resolution because key Republicans in Congress, including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, have taken a tough public stand against Beijing's rights record.

"I think that Senator (Jesse) Helms and Representative Gingrich and President (Bill) Clinton and Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright share the same concern. We're all Americans. We all want to see innocent people in China have their human rights respected. There's no partisan disagreement on this issue of human rights in China," he said.

Burns called China's decision to sign a U.N. covenant on economic, social and cultural rights a "positive step" but reiterated his statement from Tuesday that this would not dissuade the United States from backing the U.N. rights resolution.
